claim: Engineering a Compiler defines a context-free grammar formally as a quadruple (T, NT, S, P), where T is the set of terminal symbols, or words, and NT is the set of nonterminal symbols, the syntactic variables that give the productions structure.
quote: Formally, a context-free grammar G is a quadruple (T, NT, S, P) where: T is the set of terminal symbols, or words, in the language L(G). Terminal symbols correspond to syntactic categories returned by the scanner. NT is the set of nonterminal symbols. They are syntactic variables introduced to provide abstraction and structure in the productions of G.

claim: Engineering a Compiler defines a derivation as a sequence of rewriting steps that begins with the grammar's start symbol and ends with a sentence, each step picking a nonterminal in the prototype string, choosing a rule for it, and rewriting it.
quote: Derivation a sequence of rewriting steps that begins with the grammar's start symbol and ends with a sentence in the language To derive a sentence, we start with a prototype string that contains just the start symbol. We then repeat the following process: (1) pick a nonterminal symbol, α, in the prototype string; (2) choose a grammar rule, α → β; and (3) rewrite α with β.

claim: Engineering a Compiler defines a rightmost derivation as one that rewrites the rightmost nonterminal at each step, and a leftmost derivation as one that rewrites the leftmost nonterminal at each step.
quote: Rightmost derivation a derivation that rewrites, at each step, the rightmost nonterminal Leftmost derivation a derivation that rewrites, at each step, the leftmost nonterminal

locator: Section 3.2.3 'More Complex Examples', printed p. 92 (PDF p. 119)
claim: Engineering a Compiler defines a parse tree, also called a syntax tree, as a graph that represents a derivation.
quote: Parse tree a graph that represents a derivation; also called a syntax tree

claim: Engineering a Compiler defines a sentential form as a string of symbols that occurs as one step in a valid derivation.
quote: Sentential form a string of symbols that occurs as one step in a valid derivation

locator: Section 3.2.3 'More Complex Examples' (ambiguity), printed pp. 92-93 (PDF pp. 120-121)
claim: Engineering a Compiler defines a grammar G as ambiguous when some sentence in L(G) has more than one rightmost (or leftmost) derivation, equivalently more than one parse tree.
quote: A grammar G is ambiguous if some sentence in L(G) has more than one rightmost (or leftmost) derivation. Alternatively, a grammar G is ambiguous if some sentence in L(G) has more than one parse tree.

claim: Whether a given context-free grammar is ambiguous is undecidable, because deciding it would decide the undecidable Post correspondence problem.
quote: The undecidability of this problem follows from the fact that if an algorithm to determine ambiguity existed, the Post correspondence problem could be decided, which is known to be undecidable.

claim: Ambiguity is usually a feature of a grammar rather than of the language it generates: an unambiguous grammar can generate the same context-free language, though some inherently ambiguous languages can only be generated by ambiguous grammars.
quote: Usually, ambiguity is a feature of the grammar, not the language, and an unambiguous grammar can be found that generates the same context-free language. However, there are certain languages that can only be generated by ambiguous grammars; such languages are called inherently ambiguous languages.

claim: BNF emerged when John Backus proposed a metalinguistic notation for IAL (ALGOL 58) in 1959, and it was formalized in the ALGOL 60 report, where Peter Naur named it Backus normal form.
quote: BNF itself emerged when John Backus, a programming language designer at IBM, proposed a metalanguage of metalinguistic formulas to define the syntax of the new programming language IAL, known today as ALGOL 58, in 1959. This notation was formalized in the ALGOL 60 report, where Peter Naur named it Backus normal form in the committee's 1963 report.

claim: Noam Chomsky adapted Thue's formalism and in 1956 introduced the distinction between generative rules, which are the rules of context-free grammars, and transformation rules.
quote: Noam Chomsky, teaching linguistics to students of information theory at MIT combined linguistics and mathematics, adapting Thue's formalism to describe natural language syntax. In 1956, he introduced a clear distinction between generative rules (those of context-free grammars) and transformation rules.

claim: Engineering a Compiler gives an algorithm for grammars without cycles or epsilon productions that removes indirect left recursion by forward substitution and then removes direct left recursion.
quote: To eliminate all left recursion, we need a systematic approach. The algorithm in Fig. 3.6 eliminates all left recursion from a grammar by thorough application of two techniques: forward substitution to convert indirect left recursion into direct left recursion and conversion of direct left recursion to right recursion with the transformation, as before.

claim: Engineering a Compiler defines FIRST(alpha) for a grammar symbol as the set of terminals that can appear as the first word of a sentential form derived from it, with epsilon and eof included in the set's domain.
quote: For each grammar symbol α, define the set FIRST(α) as the set of terminal symbols that can appear as the first word in some sentential form derived from α. The domain of FIRST is {NT ∪ T ∪ ε ∪ eof}, the set of all grammar symbols.

claim: Engineering a Compiler defines FOLLOW(A) as the set of words that can occur immediately to the right of a string derived from A, whose members come from the terminals plus eof.
quote: To capture that knowledge of the grammar's structure, we define the set FOLLOW (A) to contain all of the words that can occur to the immediate right of a string derived from A. The domain of FOLLOW is NT and its range is T ∪ {eof}.

claim: Engineering a Compiler states that a grammar is backtrack free if and only if, for every nonterminal with multiple right-hand sides, the START sets of its alternative right-hand sides are pairwise disjoint.
quote: A grammar is backtrack free if and only if, for any nonterminal A with multiple right-hand sides, A → β1 | β2 | . . . | βn: START(A → βi) ∩ START(A → βj) = ∅, ∀ 1 ≤ i, j ≤ n, i ≠ j.

claim: Engineering a Compiler defines the augmented first set first+(A→beta) of a production to be first(beta) when epsilon is not in first(beta), and first(beta) ∪ follow(A) otherwise.
quote: For a production A → β, define its augmented first set, first+, as follows: first+(A→β) = first(β) if ε ∉ first(β); first(β) ∪ follow(A) otherwise

claim: In the name LL(1), the first L means scanning the input left to right, the second L means discovering a leftmost derivation, and the 1 means a one-symbol lookahead.
quote: The name LL(1) derives from the fact that these parsers scan their input Left to right, discover a Leftmost derivation, and use a 1 symbol lookahead.

claim: Engineering a Compiler defines left factoring as rewriting productions that share a common prefix so that the common prefix is recognized through a new nonterminal and only the distinct suffixes remain as alternatives.
quote: If a nonterminal symbol has multiple right-hand sides that share a common prefix, we can left factor the rules to shift recognition of the common prefix onto a new nonterminal symbol. The transformation takes a nonterminal and its productions: A → αβ1 | αβ2 | . . . | αβn | γ1 | γ2 | . . . | γj

claim: Bison's shift/reduce parser is a bottom-up parser.
quote:
The parser tries, by shifts and reductions, to reduce the entire input down to a single grouping whose symbol is the grammar's start-symbol (see section Languages and Context-Free Grammars).

This kind of parser is known in the literature as a bottom-up parser.

claim: Parser error recovery allows continued parsing to find more syntax errors in one compilation.
quote: A parser should find as many syntax errors as possible in each compilation. The parser needs a mechanism that lets it “recover” from an error—that is, move to a state where it can continue parsing.
